ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in $\triangle ABC$, points D, E, and F are the midpoints of the sides, respectively. If the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $16\,cm^2$, then what is the area of $\triangle DEF$ in $cm^2$?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:}

Since points D and F are the midpoints of AB and AC, respectively, \\
$\therefore$DF$\parallel $BC and DF$ = \frac{1}{2}$BC, \\
$\therefore$DF$\parallel $BE, \\
Since E is the midpoint of BC, \\
$\therefore$BE$ = \frac{1}{2}$BC, \\
$\therefore$DF$ = $BE, \\
$\therefore$Quadrilateral BEFD is a parallelogram, \\
$\therefore$BD$ = $EF, \\
In $\triangle $BDE and $\triangle $FED, \\
$ \left\{\begin{array}{l}DF=BE \\ BD=EF \\ DE=DE \end{array}\right.$ \\
$\therefore$$\triangle $BDE$\cong $$\triangle $FED \text{ (SSS)}, \\
Similarly, it can be proven that $\triangle $DAF$\cong $$\triangle $FED and $\triangle $EFC$\cong $$\triangle $FED, \\
i.e., $\triangle $BDE$\cong $$\triangle $DAF$\cong $$\triangle $EFC$\cong $$\triangle $FED, \\
$\therefore$Area of $\,\triangle $DEF$ = \frac{1}{4}$Area of $\,\triangle $ABC$ = \frac{1}{4} \times 16 = \boxed{4} \text{ (cm}^2\text{)}$.
